extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, screenwriting students, and filmmakers studying story design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for structuring a screenplay from the smallest dramatic unit (beat) through scene, sequence, act, to whole-story design, and for choosing among classical, minimalist, and anti-structure approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Event
rubrics_metrics.description: A single event in the life of the characters that can be staged in many ways; e.g., the single Story Event “lovers break up” may be told in one scene or across many scenes, cross-cut, or parsed for details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer chooses how to present a Story Event (single scene vs multiple scenes; linear vs cross-cutting) depending on what needs to be revealed about character, setting, or future story needs. Variations are endless but the underlying Story Event is the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat
rubrics_metrics.description: A BEAT is the smallest element of dramatic structure: an exchange of behavior in action/reaction (not to be confused with a dialogue-pause beat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beats are distinct changes of behavior that, beat by beat, shape the turning of a scene. Example: the lovers-break-up scene built from six beats (teasing, insults, daring, pleading/ridiculing, violence, decisive action). Each beat should show a clear change of action/reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Every true scene turns the value-charged condition of the character’s life; scenes cause relatively minor yet significant change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make each scene turn something (a value) for the character. Use beats to build the scene so behavior and action change or set up conditions for future change. Scenes can be focused on inner states or external events, but must register a value shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: A SEQUENCE is a series of scenes—generally two to five—that culminates with greater impact than any previous scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequences aggregate scene-level turns into a larger, more determinant change (the sequence climax). Title sequences to clarify why they exist (e.g., 'getting the job') and ensure the sequence as a whole arcs from one value state to another (example: NO JOB → JOB over three scenes). Sequence scenes can vary in their individual values but should subordinate to the sequence’s master value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act
rubrics_metrics.description: An ACT is a series of sequences that peaks in a climactic scene which causes a major reversal of values—more powerful than any previous sequence or scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish act-level change by its degree of impact on the character's life (inner life, relationships, fortunes). Design sequences within an act to build toward an act-climax that meaningfully reverses the protagonist’s value-charged condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story (whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is a series of acts that build to a last-act climax (story climax) which brings about absolute and irreversible change in the protagonist’s life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the value-charged condition at the story’s opening and at its end—there must be an absolute, irreversible arc. Design every level (beat → scene → sequence → act) to contribute to that final irreversible change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Climax / Closed Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: A Story Climax that answers all questions raised by the telling and satisfies all audience emotion is a CLOSED ENDING—an absolute, irreversible change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closed endings leave the audience with a rounded, satisfied experience; examples and contrast with open endings demonstrate when closure is required by design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: A Story Climax that leaves a question or two unanswered and some emotion unfulfilled is an OPEN ENDING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miniplot often uses open endings: most questions are answered but one or two trail out for the audience to resolve (e.g., PARIS, TEXAS leaves some family relationship questions to the viewer). Open endings must leave limited, answerable alternatives, not chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (writer’s choice of events and design in time)
rubrics_metrics.description: To PLOT means to navigate story terrain, choosing which events to include/exclude and their order in time; plot is the writer’s intentional selection and arrangement of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plotting is active decision-making: which events to present, what to omit, and how to order them so the story’s inner logic and arc are created. Poor choices yield weak plots; good choices create causally connected, meaningful design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archplot / Classical Design
rubrics_metrics.description: CLASSICAL DESIGN (Archplot) means a story built around an active protagonist who struggles against primarily external antagonistic forces, through continuous time, within a consistent and causally connected fictional reality, to a closed ending of absolute, irreversible change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archplot emphasizes causality, linear time, external conflict, single active protagonist, consistent reality, and a closed ending. It's the dominant, internationally successful form and accommodates vast variety while keeping these classical principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miniplot (Minimalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Miniplot begins with elements of Classical Design but reduces or compresses them—simplicity and economy while retaining enough classical structure to satisfy an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miniplot often emphasizes internal conflict, may leave some questions open, and trades the roller-coaster dynamic of Archplot for understatement, austerity, or focused inner journeys (e.g., TENDER MERCIES, FIVE EASY PIECES). It is not 'plotless'—it requires careful execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiplot (Antistructure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiplot reverses or contradicts classical principles (nonlinear time, inconsistent realities, coincidence, fragmented causality) to exploit or ridicule formal principles; often extravagant and self-conscious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiplot emphasizes disruption: scrambled time, arbitrary coincidence, inconsistent realities and symbolic or bizarre elements (examples: LAST YEAR AT MARIENBAD, UN CHIEN ANDALOU). When done well, it expresses a singular subjective perception; when done poorly, it fragments audience comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed vs Open Endings (formal contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed Ending: all story questions answered and emotions satisfied. Open Ending: one or two questions left unanswered; emotional residue remains for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose closed when the design demands resolution; choose open when you want the audience to participate in concluding the story’s implications. Ensure any open question is answerable by audience inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: External vs Internal Conflict (formal contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archplot emphasizes external conflict (protagonist vs people/institutions/physical forces). Miniplot often emphasizes internal conflict (battles in thought and feeling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the story’s dominant energy is outward struggle or inner transformation; the emphasis affects pacing, scene construction, and the kinds of events you stage (survival, social battles vs psychological journeys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single vs Multiple Protagonists (formal contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-protagonist design centers one major story and star role (Archplot). Multiplot/miniplot fragments the film among multiple protagonists and subplots (Multiplot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-protagonist stories maintain tight roller-coaster dynamics; multiplot softens intensity by distributing dramatic weight across several protagonists and stories (examples: THE FUGITIVE vs PARENTHOOD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Active vs Passive Protagonist (formal contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ACTIVE PROTAGONIST pursues desire and takes action in conflict with the world; a PASSIVE PROTAGONIST pursues desire inwardly and reacts more than forces change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active protagonists drive plot through motivated action; passive protagonists require the writer to heighten inner conflict or surround them with dramatic external events to sustain interest (examples: Archplot vs Pelle the Conqueror).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear vs Nonlinear Time (formal contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linear Time: events arranged in temporal order the audience can follow (may include flashbacks handled clearly). Nonlinear Time: time is scrambled or blurred so the audience cannot easily order events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linear designs favor clarity of causality and progression; nonlinear designs can foreground psychology, theme, or formal experiment (e.g., BAD TIMING’s salad-of-time structure), but risk confusing the audience if not disciplined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality vs Coincidence (formal contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causality: motivated actions cause effects that spawn further effects in chain-linked episodes to the Story Climax. Coincidence: unmotivated actions trigger events that do not cause further effects, fragmenting the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor causality to create interconnected meaning and arc. Use coincidence deliberately to suggest randomness, absurdity, or to subvert expectation—recognizing that coincidence tends to produce fragmentation and open endings (example: AFTER HOURS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent vs Inconsistent Realities (formal contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent Realities: the fictional world establishes and keeps interaction rules consistently to create meaning. Inconsistent Realities: modes of interaction mix so episodes jump between realities, creating a sense of absurdity or subjective expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you create story rules (even bizarre ones), adhere to them for internal coherence. Inconsistent realities (Antiplot) can serve a subjective or satirical purpose but must be handled intentionally to avoid arbitrary confusion (example: WEEKEND’s one-off insertion of Emily Brontë).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change vs Stasis (Nonplot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Change: stories that arc and produce visible change in characters. Stasis/Nonplot: narratives that remain in portraiture or equilibrium and do not arc—the character’s value-charged condition at the end is virtually identical to the opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonplot works (slice-of-life) can be powerful as portraiture or insight, but they are not traditional story arcs; be clear if you intend stasis so audience expectations are managed (examples: UMBERTO D, FACES).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical construction principle (beats→scenes→sequences→acts→story)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural hierarchy: beats build scenes; scenes build sequences; sequences build acts; acts build the whole story to its climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design at each level so that the smaller unit 'does its job': every phrase of dialogue or description either turns behavior/action or sets up conditions for change. This cumulative work serves the story’s deep purpose and final climax.
